V04-E-001: When people who share no common language must trade or work together for long periods, they often improvise a pidgin, a stripped-down tongue assembled from pieces of the languages around them. A pidgin has a small vocabulary, few grammatical endings and a loose word order, and nobody speaks it as a first language. These children do not simply copy the makeshift speech of their parents. Within a generation or two they regularise it, adding consistent markers for tense, settled rules of word order and ways of building complex sentences. The result, called a creole, is a full language in every sense, capable of expressing anything its speakers need. Linguists have long debated whether this rapid growth reveals something innate in the way children acquire language, or simply reflects the pressures of daily use. What happens next, when children are born into communities where the pidgin is the main shared language, is one of the more remarkable episodes in the life of languages.
V04-E-002: Readers outside the academy often treat footnotes as clutter, the visible residue of a scholar's anxiety to seem thorough. The complaint is understandable, since a page whose lower third is crowded with small print can feel less like an argument than like a legal contract. Yet the footnote performs a function that the main text cannot. It tells the reader exactly where a claim came from, so that anyone with patience and a library card can go and check. A historian who cites a box and folder in such an archive is, in effect, handing her critics the means to test her reading of it. Admittedly, the device can be abused: a thicket of citations can intimidate rather than inform, and some notes point to sources that do not say what they are claimed to say. But the remedy for bad footnotes is better ones, not fewer, because prose that cannot be traced to its sources asks to be trusted rather than examined. That traceability matters most where the evidence is hardest for an ordinary reader to reach, as with the unpublished papers kept in archives.
V04-E-003: It is usually said that radio drama declined because television could do everything it did and show pictures as well. The argument assumes that the absence of images was a defect, a gap that early broadcasters filled with sound effects only because they had nothing better. Those who wrote for the medium understood it differently. A listener who hears a door creak and footsteps on gravel does not receive a scene; she assembles one, drawing on every door and every path she has known. The room she imagines is therefore more particular to her than any set designer could make it, and more convincing, because she built it herself. This is why certain stories, ghost stories above all, can seem more frightening on the radio than on the screen: the monster that is never shown is shaped by each listener's private fears. None of this means that radio drama was secretly superior, only that its supposed weakness was the very source of its power, and that television replaced it without ever reproducing what it did. Television, by contrast, builds that room for her, finished down to the wallpaper, and builds the same one for every other viewer.
V04-E-004: Words coined to soften an unpleasant subject tend to have short careers. A term is introduced precisely because the older word has picked up a sting, and for a while the new one sounds neutral, even kind. But the attitudes that gave the old word its sting have not gone anywhere, and they soon attach themselves to the replacement. Within a generation the polite term is being used as a taunt in school playgrounds, and reformers begin searching for another. The cycle can be traced through the vocabulary of illness, disability and poverty, and even through the names for the lavatory, which have turned over again and again. Some observers conclude from this that the effort to find kinder words is pointless, but that does not quite follow, since a new word can at least signal that the speaker means no harm, even if the signal fades. The fair conclusion, then, is neither that renaming is futile nor that it works on its own, but that words can only announce a change in feeling that has to happen somewhere else.
V04-E-005: Memorising multiplication tables has a poor reputation among educators who want children to understand mathematics rather than recite it. The worry is reasonable, because a child can chant the tables perfectly and still have no idea when multiplication is the right tool. Yet memorised facts and understanding are not rivals, for the mind can attend to only a few things at once, and every fact that must be worked out uses up some of that limited space. A pupil who knows the fact instantly, by contrast, keeps her attention free for the question that matters, which is why the tiles need to be multiplied at all. Fluency, in other words, is not the enemy of thought but one of its conditions. None of this justifies drilling tables before children grasp what multiplication means; the case is for memorising facts that are already understood, not for memorising instead of understanding. A pupil who has to count on her fingers to find seven times eight, in the middle of a problem about the cost of tiles for a floor, will often have lost track of the problem by the time she has the answer.
V04-E-006: A long tradition in teaching holds that people learn to solve problems chiefly by solving them, struggling through difficulties until the method becomes their own. For learners who already know a good deal, that tradition is largely sound. Such learners often reach an answer by trial and error and come away with no clearer idea of the method than they had before. Studying a fully worked solution, step by step, spares them the search and directs their attention to the structure of the solution itself. The advantage does not last, however: as competence grows, the same worked examples become redundant, and learners who are made to study them gain less than those left to tackle problems on their own. The sensible conclusion is not that one method is right, but that the right method depends on where the learner stands. For genuine beginners, however, unaided struggle tends to be a poor teacher, because it consumes their attention in searching for a route rather than in noticing why the route works.
V04-E-007: Across much of the multilingual world, pupils start their schooling in a language seldom spoken in their homes, typically because it is the language of the state, the universities and the better-paid professions. The intention is to give them an early start in the language that will matter most for their futures. In practice, a child who must learn to read in an unfamiliar tongue faces two tasks at once: decoding print and making sense of words she does not yet know. The result is that many such children fall behind in the early years in a way that later teaching struggles to undo. Children who first learn to read in their home language face only the first task, and once they can read, the skill carries over to a second language with surprising ease. This is why the case for teaching in the mother tongue during the first years is not a case against the dominant language but a better route towards it. Parents who want their children taught in the language of opportunity from the first day are not wrong about where opportunity lies; they are mistaken only about the quickest way to reach it. Either task alone would tax a six-year-old, and the two together compete for the same limited attention.
V04-E-008: Few school reforms are as popular with parents and teachers as smaller classes. The appeal is intuitive: with fewer pupils, a teacher should be able to notice each child's difficulties and respond to them. The evidence, however, is more mixed than the enthusiasm suggests. Modest cuts, from thirty-two pupils to twenty-eight, say, seem to change little, perhaps because teachers carry on teaching in exactly the way they did before. Larger cuts can help, particularly for the youngest children, but they are expensive and require many new teachers, some of whom will be less experienced than those already in post. The same money might in some cases do more good if it were spent on improving the teaching that pupils already receive. Smaller classes, in short, create an opportunity for better teaching rather than guaranteeing it, and if the opportunity goes unused, that money has bought very little.
V04-E-009: For much of the twentieth century, the rise of allergies and asthma in wealthy countries puzzled doctors. One influential suggestion was that children raised in very clean surroundings meet too few microbes early in life. On this view, an immune system that is not kept busy with genuine threats begins to react against harmless things such as pollen and dust. The idea drew support from the observation that children who grow up on farms, among animals, seem less prone to allergies than children in cities. That popular version, however, went further than the evidence. The microbes that appear to matter are mostly those of soil, animals and a varied natural environment, not the germs that household cleaning removes, so the lesson is not to give up washing hands. Such findings were soon popularised as a warning that modern households had simply become too clean.
V04-E-010: Emergency departments do not treat patients in the order in which they arrive. Instead, a nurse makes a rapid assessment of each newcomer and assigns a priority based on how quickly the patient's condition is likely to worsen without help. The principle can seem unfair to those who wait, since it rewards neither patience nor punctuality. Yet the alternative, a queue in strict order of arrival, would mean that a patient whose life depended on speed might die behind a dozen who could safely have waited. Triage, in other words, does not ignore fairness but rests on a different idea of it, one that weighs the cost of waiting rather than the time already spent. Even so, a department that applies the principle well can still fail its patients by leaving them uninformed, and it is often the silence, rather than the order of treatment, that waiting patients resent. A man with a broken wrist who has waited patiently since early evening may watch a woman who arrived an hour ago with chest pain go straight through to a doctor.
V04-E-011: When hospitals began asking surgical teams to work through a short checklist before each operation, many surgeons were insulted. They did not need, they said, a printed card to remind them to confirm the patient's identity or check which side of the body was to be operated on. In one sense they were right: almost nothing on such lists is unknown to a qualified surgeon. A pause in which every member of the team introduces themselves and states a concern makes it easier for a junior nurse to point out, minutes later, that something looks wrong. In a setting where authority runs steeply from the surgeon downwards, that permission to speak can matter more than any single item on the card. It also explains a less welcome observation: where checklists are introduced as paperwork, ticked by one person in a corner, they tend to achieve very little. The card is not the cure; the conversation it forces is. But the lists were never meant to supply knowledge; their value lay in what the ritual of working through them aloud did to the people in the room.
V04-E-012: Iodine deficiency was once widespread in upland districts and in regions far from the sea, where the soil holds little of the element. Its most visible sign was goitre, a swelling of the thyroid gland in the neck, but its gravest effect was hidden: children born to deficient mothers could suffer lasting harm to their mental development. The remedy turned out to be remarkably simple. Since salt is eaten by almost everybody, in quantities that vary little from day to day, a tiny addition of iodine reaches nearly the whole population with no change of habit required. The cost is small, the taste is unaffected, and no one needs to remember to take a pill. Where such programmes have faltered, it has usually been because of lapses in production or monitoring rather than any flaw in the idea itself. Iodised salt thus stands as a model of public health at its best: a serious harm prevented quietly, cheaply and on a vast scale.
V04-E-013: Walk across almost any park and you will find them: narrow strips of bare earth cutting diagonally across the grass, worn by people who preferred a shorter route to the one the designers laid out. Some designers now wait a season or two after a park opens, watch where people actually walk, and only then pave the routes that feet have already chosen. The result is a set of paths that people use, rather than ones they ignore. The approach has its limits, since the shortest route is not always the safest, and a track worn across a fragile meadow may destroy the very thing the park exists to protect. Still, the worn strip of earth is a kind of evidence, recorded without anyone filling in a survey, about how a place is really used. A designer who ignores it is choosing to trust a drawing over the people for whom the drawing was made. Planners have traditionally treated these desire paths as a nuisance to be fenced off or replanted, but a different attitude is possible.
V04-E-014: The intuitive response to a congested road is to widen it. For a while the extra lanes do their job, and journeys that once crawled begin to flow. But the faster journey is itself an invitation. People who had avoided the road at peak hours begin to use it, some who had taken the train return to their cars, and new houses are built further out along the route because commuting from them has become bearable. Within a few years the road is often as crowded as it was before, now carrying more vehicles at much the same crawl. Neither observation shows that roads should never be built; together they show that traffic is not a fixed quantity to be accommodated, like water to be piped, but a response to the price of travelling, measured largely in time. Congestion is that price rising, and adding capacity lowers it only until demand has caught up. The reverse has sometimes been observed as well: when a major road is closed, the expected gridlock on neighbouring streets can fail to appear, as some trips are rerouted, retimed or simply abandoned.
V04-E-015: Travel inland across certain mountain ranges and the landscape can change within a few hours' drive from dripping forest to dry scrub. The cause lies in what happens to moist air when it meets the mountains. Forced upwards by the slope, the air cools, and because cool air can hold less water vapour than warm air, much of its moisture condenses and falls as rain or snow on the windward side. The lee slopes and the plains beyond, swept by this dry, sinking air, therefore lie in what geographers call a rain shadow, receiving a fraction of the rainfall that soaks the other side. Some of the world's driest regions owe their aridity less to their distance from the sea than to a range of mountains standing between them and the prevailing winds. The point is worth remembering whenever a map is read too simply, as though rainfall were a matter of latitude alone: a single ridge can matter more than hundreds of kilometres. By the time the air has crossed the crest and begins to descend on the far side, it has shed much of its water, and it grows warmer and drier as it sinks.
V04-E-016: Grids of right-angled streets are often written off as unimaginative, the work of surveyors who cared more about parcelling out land quickly than about making beautiful places. There is some truth in the charge, since a grid laid over hills and rivers without regard for them can produce streets that are absurdly steep or that end abruptly at the water. Yet the grid has virtues that its critics tend to overlook. It is easy to find one's way in, because a newcomer who knows two street names can work out how to travel between them. It offers many alternative routes, so that traffic and pedestrians are not all funnelled onto a few main roads. And because its blocks are regular, they can be divided, combined and rebuilt over centuries as uses change, without the whole plan having to be redrawn. The winding lanes of an old quarter, by contrast, may delight the visitor but tend to resist exactly this kind of gradual reinvention.
V04-E-017: For most of their history, port cities were organised around the water's edge, where ships were loaded and unloaded by large crews of dock workers. The docks, the warehouses and the streets around them formed a dense, noisy working district, closed to casual visitors but central to the city's life. The shipping container changed that arrangement within a few decades. The new terminals were therefore built downstream or on open land at the edge of the city, and the old docks fell silent. When the abandoned waterfronts were later redeveloped as promenades, museums and apartments, the change was celebrated as a return of the water to the public. There is something to that description, since few residents had ever been able to walk along the old quays. But it is a strange kind of return, in which the waterfront becomes open to everyone at precisely the moment it stops being a place where anyone works. Ships built to carry thousands of identical steel boxes needed deep berths and acres of flat ground for stacking, and the cramped quays at the heart of the old city could offer neither.
V04-E-018: Imagine a wooden ship whose planks are replaced one at a time as they rot, until after many years not a single original plank remains. Most people asked about such a case say that it is still the same ship, because the change was gradual and the ship never ceased to sail. That answer appeals to continuity: what makes something the same thing over time is an unbroken history, not the persistence of its material. Suppose that someone has quietly collected every discarded plank and, at the end, reassembles them in their original arrangement. Now there are two ships, and each has a claim: one has the unbroken history, the other has all the original material. Whichever we choose, we seem to give up something our first answer relied upon, which suggests that our ordinary idea of sameness bundles together criteria that usually agree but can come apart. The puzzle becomes sharper, however, if we add one further detail to the story.
V04-E-019: A promise is a curious thing: by uttering a few words, I bind myself to a duty that, a moment earlier, was nowhere to be found. One popular explanation is that promising creates expectations in others, who then rely on me and stand to be harmed if I let them down. Suppose I promise a dying friend to look after her garden, and she dies within the hour, before anyone else has learned of my promise. No one now expects anything of me, and no one will be disappointed if the garden runs wild. Yet most people feel that I would still be doing something wrong in breaking my word. If they are right, the obligation must rest on something beyond the harm of dashed expectations, perhaps on the trust that was placed in me at the moment I spoke, which does not lapse merely because the one who gave it can no longer check. The trouble is that this account cannot easily explain promises on which nobody relies at all, and such promises are not hard to imagine.
V04-E-020: White lies are usually defended as small kindnesses that smooth social life at no real cost to anyone. Telling a friend that a dull dinner was delightful spares her feelings, and it is hard to see whom the lie harms. The harm, if there is one, is not to be found in any single case. It accumulates, because each lie of this kind slightly lowers the value of the words used to tell it. Someone known to praise everything soon finds that her praise carries no information. None of this requires us to become blunt or cruel; there is usually something both true and kind to be said, if we take the trouble to look for it before reaching for the easy falsehood. When she tells a nervous colleague that his speech was genuinely moving, he has no way of knowing whether she means it, and the compliment he most needed is worth nothing to him.
V04-E-021: Moral philosophers are fond of strange stories: a runaway tram that can be diverted onto a side track, killing one person instead of five, or a surgeon who could save five patients by sacrificing one healthy visitor. Critics complain that such cases are too artificial to teach us anything, since real choices are never so clean. By holding fixed the number of lives at stake and varying only the manner in which they are lost, the cases let us see whether that manner matters to us morally. Many people, when asked, judge the two cases differently, accepting the diversion but recoiling from the surgeon, although each trades one life for five. That difference is a datum which any adequate theory must either explain or explain away. The critics' worry does not disappear, however: a judgement reached about a case stripped of all context may not survive the return of that context, just as a result obtained under controlled conditions may fail in the field. But the artificiality is deliberate, in the way that a laboratory is deliberately unlike the world outside it.
V04-E-022: It seems obvious that more choice is better: if a shop offers forty kinds of jam instead of six, every customer who would have been happy before can still be happy, and some will find exactly what they wanted. Yet a very wide range of options can sometimes leave people less willing to choose at all, and less satisfied with what they eventually pick. Even those who do buy are more likely to wonder whether one of the thirty-nine they rejected would have been better. The effect is not universal, and it seems weakest when people already know what they want or when the options are clearly arranged. But it is a useful reminder that choice has costs as well as benefits, paid in time, in effort and in the nagging sense of a better option missed. A shopper faced with forty jams may compare them for several minutes, grow weary of weighing small differences, and walk away with none.
V04-E-023: Economists advise that money already spent and unrecoverable should play no part in deciding what to do next. If a concert ticket cannot be refunded, the only question on a stormy evening is whether going will be more enjoyable than staying at home; the price paid is gone either way. People who follow this advice avoid a familiar trap, that of pouring further resources into a failing project simply because so much has already been invested. Past investment sometimes carries information: a firm that has spent heavily on a project may know things about its prospects that an outsider does not. And for individuals, honouring a past commitment can be a way of remaining the kind of person who finishes things, a reputation with value of its own. The error lies not in remembering what has been spent, but in letting the memory substitute for a fresh judgement about what lies ahead. Yet the rule, sound as it is, can be applied too mechanically.
V04-E-024: There is a state of mind familiar to musicians, climbers, programmers and anyone who has lost track of time while absorbed in a demanding task. Attention narrows to the task at hand, the sense of self as an anxious observer fades, and effort, though real, no longer feels like a burden. Such absorption seems to arise most readily when the challenge of the task roughly matches the skill of the person performing it. A task that is too easy breeds boredom, while one that is far too hard breeds anxiety, and neither leaves room for complete involvement. This has an encouraging implication for work and study, since it suggests that absorption is less a gift of temperament than a result of how tasks are designed. It also carries a caution: a state that feels so rewarding can be sought in activities, from gambling to endless games, that absorb us without leaving anything of value behind. Its features are oddly consistent across activities that otherwise have little in common.
V04-E-025: Most of us regard boredom as a discomfort to be ended, preferably at once, with whatever entertainment lies within reach. Yet it may have a use. The discomfort of boredom is a signal that our present activity is not engaging us, and like hunger or pain, it pushes us to do something about it. Sometimes what we do is look for a new task; sometimes, with nothing to do, the mind wanders, and wandering minds are often where new ideas and plans take shape. A child left with an empty afternoon may invent a game that no shop could have sold her. This is not an argument for imposing tedium on anyone, only for tolerating a little of it before reaching for a cure. Relieving every flicker of boredom the moment it appears may therefore remove the very pressure that drives such invention.
